pages.title: The eight weeks before release day

text.text: Stores and playlist editors need a record long before fans hear it. Work backwards from the release date, and if any step below is late, move the date rather than rush the delivery.
Eight weeks out
Masters approved by the artist, in writing. For vinyl, order a separate vinyl master; streaming masters are too loud for a lacquer cut.
Vinyl ordered from the plant. Pressing queues run eight to twelve weeks, so a record without a vinyl slot by now goes out digital first with vinyl later.
Publicist booked and the press angle agreed: why this record, why now.
Six weeks out
Catalogue number from the next in the LT sequence (year, then the release number), UPC for the release, an ISRC for every track.
Songwriter and publisher splits confirmed for every track. Missing splits are the most common reason royalties go unpaid later.
Square cover art at full size, with no website addresses or prices on it; stores refuse those.
Four weeks out
Deliver audio, art and metadata to the distributor and move the release to
Delivered to distributor
Pre-save smart link live and on the artist's profiles.
Editorial playlist pitch sent through the distributor. Pitches need one unreleased track and at least a week, ideally more.
Release week
Move the release to
Pitching
once press is out. Brief the artist on the release-day posts.
On the day, press
Mark released
on the row. The smart link button opens the page fans see.
Day 28
Fill in
Streams, first 28 days
and
Editorial and curator playlist adds
. Compare them with the record's spend:
A single with a video and a small ad budget often does more per dollar than an album campaign; plan two singles ahead of every album.
Artists judge a label by its statements. Send them on time, every period, even when the number is small and even when the artist is unrecouped.
How the split works here
Most of the roster is on a
net profit split
: the label takes its recoupable costs back out of net receipts, then splits what is left at the artist share on their row, usually 50%. A
licensing deal
pays a higher share because the artist owns the masters.
Distribution only
artists get 85%; the label keeps a fee and takes no risk.
Each period
Download the distributor's report and total net receipts per artist after the distributor's fee.
Make a statement row per artist at
Draft
, linked to the artist, with the period end date, net receipts and the artist share.
Check it against Release costs: only costs ticked
Recoupable
come off the artist's side. Pressing is usually the label's own cost.
Send it and move the row to
Sent
. The artist's
Earned to date
counts it from that moment.
When a payment goes out, press
Mark paid
on the statement.
Recoupment, in plain words
An advance is paid back from the artist's share, never from their pocket. Until earnings pass the advance, the artist is unrecouped and receives a statement but no cheque.
Rules
Never net one artist's costs against another's earnings.
A statement in Draft for more than two weeks after the period ends shows on the Dashboard; clear it before anything else.
When an artist leaves the roster, keep paying statements for their releases for as long as the label sells them.
The label's year at a glance. Space releases at least two weeks apart so each one gets its own press and playlist push.
Costs waiting on a decision
A small label signs few artists and keeps them. This is how we go from a demo we love to a signed deal both sides understand, in our own plain-words deal memo.
Before an offer
See them play live at least once, and ask how they would feel touring for three weeks.
Check what they already own: masters of earlier releases, any existing distribution deal, and who wrote the songs.
Talk to their manager, if they have one, before talking money.

text.text: What the memo says
What we release: the songs or the record, and the format.
The split, as the artist's percentage, and what is recoupable (we list mastering, pressing, PR and video).
The advance, if any, and that it is recouped from the artist's share only.
Term, and the option for the next record.
Statements twice a year, sent even when unrecouped.
What happens if we stop working: rights revert after a set time if a record is never released.
After signing
Artist added with the deal, split and advance
First release added and costs quoted
Signed memo saved on the artist's page
Tell them, in writing, the one thing we will never do: net one artist's costs against another's earnings.
